card.name: Condong
card.tagline: The sharp, spirited palace maidservant who heralds the court legong of Bali.
card.profile: Condong is a classical Balinese court dance that originated in the mid-19th century palaces of Bali, functioning primarily as an energetic preface to legong performances. Portraying a capricious and devoted palace maidservant, the dancer enters the stage first with sharp, intense movements accompanied by semar pangulingan gamelan. The choreography features simplified forms of intricate legong movements, making it a cornerstone for training children in Balinese dance technique. In complete narrative cycles like Legong Lasem, the condong dancer also later assumes the dramatic role of a raven with wings to foretell King Lasem's death.
card.insight: Born from a 19th-century Sukawati prince's fever dream of two dancing nymphs, Condong became the foundational, intense maidservant dance taught to young Balinese girls.

card.profile_long:
Originating in the royal palaces of Bali in the mid-19th century, Condong arose as an introduction to court dance suites, created for the pleasure of Balinese royal families. Folk history attributes its origins to a prince of Sukawati who, while deathly ill, experienced a feverish vision of two celestial nymphs (bidadari) named Supraba and Wilotama dancing with consummate grace to gamelan music. Upon regaining his health, the prince recreated this vision. By the 1930s, the mythological narrative transformed into a secular court drama depicting a king or queen and their loyal subject. The character of the condong remains one of the foundational stock figures across traditional Balinese theater, appearing in gambuh and arja dramas as well as introducing legendary princesses ranging from Rangkesari to Shakespearean figures like Ophelia and Miranda.

In dramatic performance, the condong dancer enters the stage first before the primary legong dancers appear. Typically performed by a young girl, the dance lasts approximately 15 minutes and features movements described by ethnomusicologist Michael Tenzer as remarkably sharp and intense. The choreography depicts the daily activities and whims of a capricious young court servant who is in awe of the king's royal power and the beauty of his daughter. When the main legong performance begins, the condong dancer dances with the incoming performers, presents each dancer with a fan, and then withdraws. In the extended drama of Legong Lasem (also referred to as Legong Kraton), the same dancer returns to the stage equipped with raven wings to portray an omen of death that foretells the demise of King Lasem.

The dance is traditionally accompanied by the antique semar pangulingan style of gamelan, or specialized historic ensembles such as the Semara Patangian orchestra maintained by conservation centers like Mekar Bhuana. The musical accompaniment consists of a cycle of short 16-beat melodies organized in the gegaboran meter. When Condong serves as the direct preface to legong kraton, the musical suite concludes with an accelerating shift into the batel meter, matching the sudden dramatic transition as the maidservant delivers props and yields the floor to the royal protagonists.

Because the choreography condenses and simplifies the fundamental vocabulary of legong, Condong serves as an essential training foundation across Bali. Young children study its exacting patterns, competing in regional competitions to test their technique and earn points. Influential masters such as Ni Ketut Arini, Ni Reneng of Kedaton, and I.G.A. Susilawati have perpetuated the tradition through generations of dancers, including Putu Evie Suyadnyani. The core movements of Condong have also served as the structural basis for modern choreographies, including I Wayan Berata's 1971 welcome dance, Panyembrama.

sections.origins_and_history: The condong dance originated in the royal palaces of Bali during the mid-19th century. Although its specific historical creator is unknown, Balinese folk tradition recounts that an acutely ill prince of Sukawati witnessed a vision of two beautiful nymphs (bidadari), Supraba and Wilotama, dancing gracefully to gamelan music. Following his recovery, the prince recreated the dance. By the 1930s, the original mythological narrative was modified to tell the story of a monarch and their palace subject. In the early 20th century, it was further adapted as an introduction to legong dances staged for royal audiences.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The condong dancer enters the stage solo before the legong begins, moving with an intense and sharp dynamic quality. The routine depicts a capricious maidservant attending to court life and admiring royal majesty. As the legong performers enter, the condong dancer dances alongside them, hands each a fan, and withdraws. In the Legong Lasem drama, she later re-enters wearing raven wings to foretell the death of the king. Condong runs approximately 15 minutes and consists of fast, lively, and simplified legong movement vocabularies.
sections.music_and_instruments: Condong is accompanied by the semar pangulingan style of gamelan, as well as antique ensembles such as the Semara Patangian orchestra. The musical composition features a sequence of short 16-beat melodic structures played in the gegaboran meter. In versions serving as the preface to legong kraton, the music concludes with a rhythmic shift into batel meter.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance is performed on court stages, theater spaces, and modern concert halls. Dancers wear traditional Balinese court dance attire appropriate for female palace roles, carry hand fans to present to the subsequent dancers, and don raven wings when enacting the omen in Legong Lasem.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Traditionally danced for the pleasure of Balinese royal families, Condong introduces royal legong, gambuh, and arja theatrical suites. It portrays the devotion, awe, and daily duties of a palace maidservant serving her sovereign. Today, it also features in youth dance competitions, preservation festivals, and international conservatory showcases.
sections.notable_figures: Choreographer and teacher Ni Ketut Arini; master instructors Ni Reneng of Kedaton and I.G.A. Susilawati; choreographer I Wayan Berata (who adapted condong movements into Panyembrama in 1971); and dancer Putu Evie Suyadnyani of Mekar Bhuana Conservatory.
sections.regional_variants: The dance originated in Sukawati and is preserved in major Balinese court traditions including Kedaton and Sanur. It manifests in specialized theatrical formats such as Legong Kraton / Legong Lasem, gambuh, and arja.
sections.lineage: Derived from royal 19th-century court dances and legong prototypes; gave rise to the 1971 modern classic Panyembrama choreographed by I Wayan Berata, and continues as a foundational teaching tool in contemporary Balinese conservatories.

music_profile.meter: 16-beat gegaboran meter shifting to batel meter
music_profile.musical_form: Cyclic 16-beat gegaboran melody concluding with batel transition
music_profile.sound_description: A refined, vibrant Balinese gamelan sound characterized by the crystalline resonance of semar pangulingan metallurgy, executing short 16-beat melodic periods in gegaboran meter that accelerate and transition sharply into the driving batel meter.

movement_profile.footwork: Simplified versions of legong footwork executed with sharp and intense precision
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Hand gestures manipulating and presenting fans to subsequent dancers
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Solo floor entrance traversing the stage, culminating in a shared space with legong dancers before exit
movement_profile.partnering: Presents hand fans to incoming legong dancers while dancing in unison or coordination

signature_moves.name: Fan presentation
signature_moves.description: Dancing with the incoming legong performers and handing a fan to each dancer before withdrawing.

signature_moves.name: Raven omen dance
signature_moves.description: Re-entering the stage wearing raven wings to foretell the death of King Lasem.

movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid sluggish or loose movements, maintaining the sharp, lively, and intense precision characteristic of Balinese female court dance.

episode_brief.logline: Before the queens of Balinese legong take the stage, a young girl portraying a nimble maidservant commands the palace floor with razor-sharp grace.
beats: A 19th-century Sukawati prince awakens from illness and records his vision of two dancing bidadari.
A young dancer prepares behind the curtain, donning the regalia of the royal maidservant.
The semar pangulingan gamelan strikes a 16-beat gegaboran meter as the condong makes her solo entrance.
Through fast, intense movements, she enacts the awe and daily routine of palace service.
The legong dancers arrive; she presents them their fans with courtly precision.
In the Lasem drama, she reappears with black raven wings, casting the fateful omen across the court.

lesson_ladder.goal: Internalize the 16-beat gegaboran rhythm and lively stance.
drills: Count through the 16-beat cycle with gamelan accompaniment.
Practice holding the intense, focused gaze required of the condong maidservant.
Execute basic entrance steps to the opening melodic phrase.

lesson_ladder.goal: Coordinate sharp movement transitions and prop handoffs.
drills: Drill the sharp, sudden directional shifts characteristic of the routine.
Rehearse the ceremonial grip and presentation of the fan.
Coordinate step timing during the transition into batel meter.

lesson_ladder.goal: Sustain the 15-minute choreography with stamina and dramatic presence.
drills: Execute the full 15-minute solo endurance run.
Coordinate spatial transitions with two incoming legong partners.
Perform the dramatic raven-wing omen sequence for Legong Lasem.

episode_brief.instructor_persona: An exacting Balinese conservatory master like Putu Evie Suyadnyani, instilling courtly discipline and vivid expressive intensity in young performers.
episode_brief.music_cue: Antique Semara Patangian gamelan ringing in cyclical 16-beat gegaboran meter before breaking into rapid batel meter.

connections.name: Legong
connections.note: Condong features simplified versions of legong movements and serves as its traditional introductory preface.

connections.name: Legong Lasem
connections.note: In Legong Lasem (Legong Kraton), the condong dancer returns wearing raven wings to foretell the king's doom.

connections.name: Panyembrama
connections.note: Created in 1971 by I Wayan Berata, incorporating adapted movements from Condong and Legong.

connections.name: Gambuh
connections.note: Shares the condong stock maidservant character.

connections.name: Arja
connections.note: Also incorporates the stock condong maidservant figure.

seniors.seated_version: Perform the maidservant's upper-body gestures and fan presentations seated upright in a stable chair, following the 16-beat melodic count.
seniors.standing_version: Execute modified, low-impact upper-body gestures while standing with chair support, maintaining gentle posture without deep knee bends.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Reduce tempo by half and restrict arm extensions to a comfortable, pain-free range.
seniors.counts: Keep a steady 4-count or 8-count pulse instead of the demanding 16-beat cycle.

children.game_version: The Royal Messenger game: children carry and hand off fans to partners on count 16 without dropping the rhythm.
children.counts: Count aloud in sets of 4 up to 16 beats matching the gamelan gong cycles.

observation.setting: In front of an ornate traditional carved wooden door and Balinese stone architecture, on a tiled floor.
observation.formation_and_space: Solo performance staying centrally framed in front of the doorway, occasionally moving laterally or kneeling in place.
observation.posture: Low stance with deeply bent knees (alit/ageng posture), weight shifted between legs, torso held upright or leaning dynamically.
observation.footwork: Balancing on balls of feet, rapid weight shifts, crouching steps, and knee drops aligned with percussive accents in the music.
observation.arms_and_hands: Arms held out with elbows raised, fingers hyperextended in classical Balinese gestures (pelinggih/tawa-tawa), articulating intricate hand and wrist movements.
observation.hips_and_torso: Sharp hip drops and side-to-side torso shifts coordinated with the gamelan beats and eye movements.
observation.levels_jumps_turns: Transitions between standing low stances, deep squats, and kneeling on the floor.
observation.costume_and_props: Traditional Balinese costume consisting of a magenta patterned wrap skirt (stagen/kain), dark sash, white top with crossed pink sash, hair pulled back with ornaments.
observation.cannot_infer: Precise foot-to-floor contact details and subtle finger tremors are obscured by video resolution.

signature_moments.what: Low stance shifting side to side with extended arms and rapid eye movements (nyeledet).
Deep squat while rapidly crossing arms in front and tossing head side to side.
